units.unit: Tighter rent control would help SDU tenants stay in their homes
Needs sources backing the claim and a source showing the other side
D11 surveys tenants and discusses tenure security, fitting the claim about staying in homes
D2 has rent and stock numbers to ground the claim in data
Tenants care more about security of tenure than rent level
Tightening should focus on tenure security, not hard caps
D2 shows stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance
D5 is the landlord side
D7 is Berlin's rent cap
D5 and D7 show the opposing case about supply shrinking that must be answered
Hong Kong should tighten protection for SDU tenants through tenure security and inspection, not a hard rent cap
D11 says tenants would trade rent for security and the real problem is queue length
D7 shows Berlin's cap shrank listings
D2 shows stock kept growing under the moderate 2021 ordinance
Rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent even under the ordinance, which only capped increases
This shows the ordinance was too weak on initial rents, not that caps are the answer
A hard cap on initial rents would shrink supply, hurting people still outside
Doing nothing is not acceptable because tenants have no written agreements and the ordinance left initial rents alone
Enforcement would miss the most exploited tenants since inspection covers little of the stock
D6 gives the supply elasticity numbers behind the claim that a hard cap shrinks supply
D4 is a tenant with no written agreement for the claim that doing nothing is not acceptable
D10 is the enforcement minute for the claim that inspection would miss the most exploited tenants
Landlords would convert cubicles to storage rather than take regulated tenants, which a landlord voice should confirm
The 2021 ordinance capped increases but left initial rents unregulated
The people the ordinance was meant to protect are new arrivals
The ordinance text should show it only capped increases within a tenancy and not initial rents
The consultation should show who the policy targets, which is new arrivals
The consultation should show any package the government signalled
The landlord interview should show landlords converting units to storage instead of renting to regulated tenants
D1 should show the 2021 ordinance capped increases but not initial rents and who it targets
D12 should show the policy package the government signalled in the consultation
A landlord voice is still missing, ideally an interview with a landlord named Mr Chan
The legal text or ruling on whether an initial rent band counts as rate-capping rather than confiscation is still missing
The landlord account should come first
The landlord source needs to show a landlord saying he would convert cubicles to storage rather than rent to regulated tenants
The legal source needs to show a published per-square-foot band on initial rents is rate-capping rather than confiscation
D3 is Mr Chan, a tenant, so I will check what he says about landlords and the waiting list
D9 is the legal opinion on whether a per-square-foot band is rate-capping rather than confiscation
A hard cap would shrink supply and the cost lands on people outside, per D6, D7 and Mr Chan's fear in D3
Doing nothing is also bad because Mrs Wong has no written tenancy and the ordinance left initial rents alone, per D4, D1, D9
Enforcement would miss the most exploited tenants because inspection covers under 6 percent and those with no agreement cannot complain, per D10
I partly agree with D5, which is why I do not back a hard cap
D9 says a hard cap risks compensation claims
D6 shows contraction
D2 shows stock kept growing under the second-generation ordinance
D9 says a published band is defensible as rate-capping
A band plus tenure security answers the exit worry better than a hard cap or doing nothing
